title: Τεύχεα Πηλεΐωνος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Zeus, watching Hector arm himself in Achilles’ armour, pities him: his death is near, and Andromache will never receive the armour from him, but for now Zeus will give him great strength. He nods, the armour fits Hector, and Ares enters him. Hector goes through the allies, names their captains and rallies them with a promise: whoever drags Patroclus’ body to the Trojans shares the spoils and the glory with him. They charge, and Ajax, fearing for himself and Menelaus, sends Menelaus to call the Argive leaders. Menelaus shouts for the chiefs, and the lesser Ajax, Idomeneus and Meriones answer. The Trojans roar on like the sea at a river mouth; the Achaeans ring the body behind their shields, and Zeus pours mist over them. The Achaeans give ground, then Ajax wheels them round and scatters the Trojans like a boar among dogs.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἀπάνευθεν ἴδεν νεφεληγερέτα Ζεὺς
τεύχεσι Πηλεΐδαο κορυσσόμενον θείοιο,
κινήσας ῥα κάρη προτὶ ὃν μυθήσατο θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hōs oun apaneuthen iden nephelēgereta Zeus
teuchesi Pēleïdao koryssomenon theioio,
kinēsas rha karē proti hon mythēsato thymon·
sentences.l:
Him then, as from apart he saw, cloud-gatherer Zeus,
in the armour of divine Peleus’-son arming himself,
having shaken, then, his head, to his own heart he spoke:
sentences.i: And when Zeus who gathers the clouds saw him from a distance, arming himself in the armour of the divine son of Peleus, he shook his head and spoke to his own heart:
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is Hector, and Zeus watches the arming from afar (ἀπάνευθεν ‘from apart’, ‘from a distance’). νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς is the stock ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’; νεφεληγερέτα is a nominative in -α. Πηλεΐδαο θείοιο is ‘of divine Peleus’-son’, Achilles, with the epic genitive -αο; κορυσσόμενον ‘arming himself’ is a present middle participle. ὃν in the last line is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative: Zeus speaks to his own heart, and what he says follows.

sentences.t:
ἆ δείλ’ οὐδέ τί τοι θάνατος καταθύμιός ἐστιν
ὃς δή τοι σχεδὸν εἶσι·
sentences.tr:
a deil’ oude ti toi thanatos katathymios estin
hos dē toi schedon eisi·
sentences.l:
“Oh, miserable one, not at all is death in-your-heart for you,
which indeed is coming near you;
sentences.i: “Oh, miserable man, death is not on your mind at all, and yet it is coming close to you;
sentences.n: ἆ δείλ’ is a cry of address, ‘oh, miserable one’, with the vocative δειλέ losing its last vowel; Zeus pities Hector for what he cannot see. καταθύμιος (κατά + θυμός) says that death is not ‘in his heart’, that is, not on his mind; the exact shade of the word is not known for certain, and ‘on your mind’ fits the line. ὃς is the relative, pointing back to θάνατος, and εἶσι is the present of εἶμι ‘go, come’.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἄμβροτα τεύχεα δύνεις
ἀνδρὸς ἀριστῆος, τόν τε τρομέουσι καὶ ἄλλοι·
sentences.tr:
sy d’ ambrota teuchea dyneis
andros aristēos, ton te tromeousi kai alloi·
sentences.l:
but you are putting on deathless armour
of a man among the best, before whom others too tremble;
sentences.i: and you are putting on the deathless armour of a man among the best, one before whom others too tremble;
sentences.n: σὺ δ’ sets Hector against the death he does not see: ‘but you…’. δύνεις is the present of δύνω ‘put on’, a continuing action, and ἄμβροτα ‘deathless’ is said of armour given by gods. ἀριστῆος is the genitive of ἀριστεύς ‘best man, champion’; the man is Achilles, not yet named. τρομέουσι is Homeric τρομέω ‘tremble before’, taking the accusative τόν, and καὶ ἄλλοι ‘others too’ says that even other men dread him.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δὴ ἑταῖρον ἔπεφνες ἐνηέα τε κρατερόν τε,
τεύχεα δ’ οὐ κατὰ κόσμον ἀπὸ κρατός τε καὶ ὤμων
εἵλευ·
sentences.tr:
tou dē hetairon epephnes enēea te krateron te,
teuchea d’ ou kata kosmon apo kratos te kai ōmōn
heileu·
sentences.i: whose companion you killed, kindly and strong, and whose armour you took, not as was fitting, from head and shoulders;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘whose’ points back to the man of 203, Achilles, and ἑταῖρον is Patroclus, ‘companion’. ἔπεφνες is the aorist of φένω ‘slay’, with a doubled stem, and ἐνηέα ‘kindly’ and κρατερόν ‘strong’ are the table’s words for him. οὐ κατὰ κόσμον is ‘not in due order’, that is, not as is fitting. κρατός is the epic genitive of κάρη ‘head’. The armour Hector stripped from Patroclus’ head and shoulders was Achilles’ own, which Patroclus had been wearing.

sentences.t: ἀτάρ τοι νῦν γε μέγα κράτος ἐγγυαλίξω,
sentences.tr: atar toi nyn ge mega kratos engyalixō,
sentences.l: but now, at least, to you great strength I will put into the hand,
sentences.i: but for now, at least, I will put great strength into your hands,
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ and νῦν γε ‘for now at least’ turn from Hector’s fault to what Zeus will give him. ἐγγυαλίξω is ‘I will put into the hand, deliver’, from ἐγγυαλίζω. κράτος is ‘strength’; the gift is the strength that fills Hector in the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
τῶν ποινὴν ὅ τοι οὔ τι μάχης ἐκνοστήσαντι
δέξεται Ἀνδρομάχη κλυτὰ τεύχεα Πηλεΐωνος.
sentences.tr:
tōn poinēn ho toi ou ti machēs eknostēsanti
dexetai Andromachē klyta teuchea Pēleïōnos.
sentences.l:
in requital for those things, that from you, in no way come home from the battle,
will Andromache receive the famous armour of Peleus’ son.”
sentences.i: in requital for those things, because you will not come home from the battle, and Andromache will not receive from you the famous armour of the son of Peleus.”
sentences.n: τῶν ‘for those things’ looks back to the armour wrongly taken from Patroclus, and ποινή is ‘requital’. ὅ is the neuter ‘that, in that’, not the relative ὅς. τοι is ‘from you’, and ἐκνοστήσαντι ‘having come home out of’ (aorist participle) agrees with it; οὔ τι negates the whole, so Hector will not return and Andromache, his wife, will not receive Achilles’ armour from him as a victor’s prize. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ κυανέῃσιν ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσε Κρονίων.
sentences.tr: ē kai kyaneēisin ep’ ophrysi neuse Kroniōn.
sentences.l: He spoke, and on his dark brows nodded the son of Cronus;
sentences.i: So he said, and the son of Cronus nodded with his dark brows;
sentences.n: ἦ καί ‘he spoke, and’ is a stock opening. The same line stands at 1.528, where the nod seals Zeus’ promise to Thetis; here it seals what he has just said. κυανέῃσιν ‘dark’ goes with ὀφρύσι ‘brows’, and νεῦσε is the aorist of νεύω ‘nod’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορι δ’ ἥρμοσε τεύχε’ ἐπὶ χροΐ, δῦ δέ μιν Ἄρης
δεινὸς ἐνυάλιος,
sentences.tr:
Hektori d’ hērmose teuche’ epi chroï, dy de min Arēs
deinos enyalios,
sentences.l:
And to Hector he fitted the armour on his skin, and entered him Ares,
dread Enyalius,
sentences.i: He fitted the armour to Hector’s skin, and Ares, the dread Enyalius, entered into him,
sentences.n: The subject of ἥρμοσε ‘fitted’ is Zeus, who after the nod of 209 is left unnamed; ἐπὶ χροΐ is ‘on the skin’. δῦ is the unaugmented aorist of δύω, here intransitive ‘entered’, with μιν ‘him’ (Hector). Ἄρης δεινὸς ἐνυάλιος: the edition prints ἐνυάλιος with a small letter, as an epithet, but it is the war-god’s other name, Enyalius; δεινός ‘dread’ is the table’s word.

sentences.t:
πλῆσθεν δ’ ἄρα οἱ μέλε’ ἐντὸς
ἀλκῆς καὶ σθένεος·
sentences.tr:
plēsthen d’ ara hoi mele’ entos
alkēs kai stheneos·
sentences.l:
and were filled, then, his limbs within
with might and strength;
sentences.i: and his limbs within were filled with might and strength;
sentences.n: πλῆσθεν is an unaugmented aorist passive, third plural (Attic ἐπλήσθησαν), ‘were filled’, with the plural neuter μέλε’ (= μέλεα ‘limbs’) as subject. οἱ ‘his’ is a dative of possession, and ἐντός means ‘within’. ἀλκῆς καὶ σθένεος are genitives after the verb of filling, ‘might’ and ‘strength’ as in the table.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δὲ κλειτοὺς ἐπικούρους
βῆ ῥα μέγα ἰάχων·
sentences.tr:
meta de kleitous epikourous
bē rha mega iachōn·
sentences.l:
and among the famous allies
he went, then, shouting greatly;
sentences.i: and he went among the famous allies, crying out loudly;
sentences.n: μετά with the accusative means ‘among’, and κλειτούς ‘famous’ (= κλυτούς) with ἐπικούρους ‘allies’ is the table’s phrase. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘went’, and ἰάχων is the present participle of ἰάχω ‘cry out’; ῥα is a light ‘then’.

sentences.t:
ἰνδάλλετο δέ σφισι πᾶσι
τεύχεσι λαμπόμενος μεγαθύμου Πηλεΐωνος.
sentences.tr:
indalleto de sphisi pasi
teuchesi lampomenos megathymou Pēleïōnos.
sentences.l:
and he appeared to them all
shining in the armour of great-hearted Peleus’ son.
sentences.i: and to all of them he appeared, gleaming in the armour of great-hearted Peleus’ son.
sentences.n: ἰνδάλλετο is the imperfect of ἰνδάλλομαι ‘appear, show oneself’; the word can mean ‘look like’, and the line lets the allies see Hector in Achilles’ shape. σφισι is the epic dative plural ‘to them’, and λαμπόμενος ‘gleaming’ a middle participle of λάμπω. τεύχεσι is dative of respect, ‘in the armour’; μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ is the table’s epithet, and Πηλεΐωνος ‘of Peleus’ son’ is Achilles.

sentences.t:
ὄτρυνεν δὲ ἕκαστον ἐποιχόμενος ἐπέεσσι
Μέσθλην τε Γλαῦκόν τε Μέδοντά τε Θερσίλοχόν τε
Ἀστεροπαῖόν τε Δεισήνορά θ’ Ἱππόθοόν τε
Φόρκυν τε Χρομίον τε καὶ Ἔννομον οἰωνιστήν·
sentences.tr:
otrynen de hekaston epoichomenos epeessi
Mesthlēn te Glaukon te Medonta te Thersilochon te
Asteropaion te Deisēnora th’ Hippothoon te
Phorkyn te Chromion te kai Ennomon oiōnistēn·
sentences.l:
And he urged on each, going among them with words,
Mesthles and Glaucus and Medon and Thersilochus,
Asteropaeus and Deisenor and Hippothous,
Phorcys and Chromius and Ennomus the bird-diviner;
sentences.i: And he went among them and urged on each man with words: Mesthles and Glaucus and Medon and Thersilochus, Asteropaeus and Deisenor and Hippothous, Phorcys and Chromius and Ennomus the reader of birds;
sentences.n: The subject of ὄτρυνεν ‘urged on’ is Hector, and ἕκαστον ‘each one’ is then named, man by man, in the three lines that follow; they are Trojan allies. Glaucus is the Lycian who has just taunted Hector in the previous part. ἐποιχόμενος is ‘going among’, ἐπέεσσι the epic dative plural ‘with words’. οἰωνιστής is ‘bird-diviner’, a man who reads the future from the flight of birds, as of Ennomus at 2.858.

sentences.t: τοὺς ὅ γ’ ἐποτρύνων ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: tous ho g’ epotrynōn epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: Them he, urging on, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Urging them on, he spoke winged words to them:
sentences.n: A stock line of speech introduction. ἐποτρύνων ‘urging on’ is a present participle; ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is a fixed phrase, translated every time; προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. ὅ γ’ is the article as pronoun, ‘he’, with γε.

sentences.t: κέκλυτε μυρία φῦλα περικτιόνων ἐπικούρων·
sentences.tr: keklyte myria phyla periktionōn epikourōn·
sentences.l: “Hear, countless tribes of neighbouring allies;
sentences.i: “Hear me, countless tribes of neighbouring allies;
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is the imperative of an old perfect, ‘hear!’, the usual call for attention. μυρία ‘countless’, φῦλα ‘tribes’ and περικτιόνων ‘dwelling around’, so ‘neighbouring’, with ἐπικούρων ‘allies’: Hector addresses all his allies at once. The speech runs to 232.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγὼ πληθὺν διζήμενος οὐδὲ χατίζων
ἐνθάδ’ ἀφ’ ὑμετέρων πολίων ἤγειρα ἕκαστον,
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō plēthyn dizēmenos oude chatizōn
enthad’ aph’ hymeterōn poliōn ēgeira hekaston,
sentences.l:
for not I, seeking a multitude, nor needing one,
here from your cities did I gather each,
sentences.i: for it was not seeking a multitude, nor needing one, that I gathered each of you here from your cities,
sentences.n: πληθύν is ‘a multitude’, sheer numbers. διζήμενος ‘seeking’ and χατίζων ‘needing’ are present participles, and ὑμετέρων ‘your’ is plural, for the allies’ own cities. ἤγειρα is here the aorist of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, though it is spelled like the aorist of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’ at 261. The sentence turns at 223 with ἀλλ’ ἵνα ‘but so that’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἵνα μοι Τρώων ἀλόχους καὶ νήπια τέκνα
προφρονέως ῥύοισθε φιλοπτολέμων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hina moi Trōōn alochous kai nēpia tekna
prophroneōs rhyoisthe philoptolemōn hyp’ Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
but so that for me the wives of the Trojans and their infant children
you may protect readily from the war-loving Achaeans.
sentences.i: but so that you may readily protect for me the wives and little children of the Trojans from the war-loving Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἵνα ‘but so that’ gives Hector’s real purpose. ῥύοισθε is an optative of ῥύομαι ‘protect’, and the optative follows the past tense of ἤγειρα. μοι ‘for me’ is a dative of interest; ἀλόχους ‘wives’ and νήπια τέκνα ‘infant children’. προφρονέως is the table’s ‘readily’, and φιλοπτολέμων ‘war-loving’ is φίλος + πτόλεμος, the Homeric form of πόλεμος. ὑπό with the genitive means ‘from’ after a verb of protecting.

sentences.t:
τὰ φρονέων δώροισι κατατρύχω καὶ ἐδωδῇ
λαούς,
sentences.tr:
ta phroneōn dōroisi katatrychō kai edōdēi
laous,
sentences.l:
Thinking on these things, with gifts I wear down and with food
the peoples,
sentences.i: With this in mind I am wearing the people down with gifts and with food,
sentences.n: τὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking on these things’, that is, ‘with this in mind’, picking up the purpose just stated. κατατρύχω ‘wear down, use up’ is the present, and δώροισι and ἐδωδῇ ‘with gifts and food’ say what drains them. λαούς ‘peoples’ are Hector’s own Trojans, whose stores supply the allies.

sentences.t: ὑμέτερον δὲ ἑκάστου θυμὸν ἀέξω.
sentences.tr: hymeteron de hekastou thymon aexō.
sentences.l: and the spirit of each one of you I make grow.
sentences.i: and I make the spirit of each of you grow.
sentences.n: ὑμέτερον ‘your’ agrees with θυμόν ‘spirit’, while ἑκάστου ‘of each’ is a genitive set beside it: ‘your spirit, each man’s’. ἀέξω is ‘make grow, raise up’ (Attic αὐξάνω); the gifts and food are meant to raise the allies’ courage.

sentences.t:
τώ τις νῦν ἰθὺς τετραμμένος ἢ ἀπολέσθω
ἠὲ σαωθήτω·
sentences.tr:
tō tis nyn ithys tetrammenos ē apolesthō
ēe saōthētō·
sentences.l:
So then let a man now, turned straight, either perish
or be saved;
sentences.i: So now let any man turn straight at the foe and either perish or be saved;
sentences.n: τώ (Attic τῷ) ‘so, therefore’ draws the conclusion from the reason just given. τετραμμένος is the perfect passive participle of τρέπω ‘turn’, with ἰθύς ‘straight’; the Greek does not say ‘at the foe’, which the English adds. ἀπολέσθω ‘let him perish’ (aorist middle) and σαωθήτω ‘let him be saved’ (aorist passive of σαόω) are third-person imperatives, ἢ … ἠέ ‘either … or’.

sentences.t: ἣ γὰρ πολέμου ὀαριστύς.
sentences.tr: hē gar polemou oaristys.
sentences.l: for this is the intimate talk of war.
sentences.i: for this is war’s intimate talk.
sentences.n: ἣ is the feminine pronoun ‘this’, agreeing with ὀαριστύς, and γάρ gives the reason a man must turn to meet it. ὀαριστύς ‘intimate talk’ is the table’s word, used at 14.216 of lovers; here it is turned bitterly to close fighting, the way war ‘converses’ with men.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κε Πάτροκλον καὶ τεθνηῶτά περ ἔμπης
Τρῶας ἐς ἱπποδάμους ἐρύσῃ, εἴξῃ δέ οἱ Αἴας,
sentences.tr:
hos de ke Patroklon kai tethnēōta per empēs
Trōas es hippodamous erysēi, eixēi de hoi Aias,
sentences.l:
But whoever Patroclus, even though dead, all the same
to the horse-taming Trojans shall drag, and Ajax give way to him,
sentences.i: and whoever drags Patroclus, dead though he is, all the same to the Trojans, tamers of horses, and Ajax gives way to him,
sentences.n: ὃς δέ κε with a subjunctive (ἐρύσῃ, εἴξῃ) is a general ‘whoever’ clause, a promise open to anyone. τεθνηῶτα, the perfect participle of θνῄσκω, means ‘dead’, and καί … περ is ‘even though’; ἔμπης is ‘all the same’. ἐρύσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐρύω ‘drag’ and εἴξῃ that of εἴκω ‘give way’; οἱ ‘to him’ is whoever succeeds. The main clause comes in the next line. The Ajax here is Telamon’s son.

sentences.t:
ἥμισυ τῷ ἐνάρων ἀποδάσσομαι, ἥμισυ δ’ αὐτὸς
ἕξω ἐγώ·
sentences.tr:
hēmisy tōi enarōn apodassomai, hēmisy d’ autos
hexō egō·
sentences.l:
half to him of the spoils I will apportion, and half myself
I will keep;
sentences.i: I will give him half of the spoils and keep half myself;
sentences.n: τῷ ‘to him’ is the article as pronoun, taking up the ὅς of 229. ἐνάρων is the genitive of ἔναρα ‘spoils’ stripped from a dead enemy, partitive after ἥμισυ ‘half’. ἀποδάσσομαι ‘I will apportion’ and ἕξω ‘I will keep’ are futures; the pronoun ἐγώ stresses that Hector himself makes the offer.

sentences.t: τὸ δέ οἱ κλέος ἔσσεται ὅσσον ἐμοί περ.
sentences.tr: to de hoi kleos essetai hosson emoi per.
sentences.l: and that glory will be for him as much as for me.”
sentences.i: and his glory will be as great as mine.”
sentences.n: τό here is the article ‘that’ (‘that glory’), and οἱ ‘for him’. ὅσσον ἐμοί περ is ‘as much as for me indeed’, with περ strengthening: the man’s fame will equal Hector’s own. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἰθὺς Δαναῶν βρίσαντες ἔβησαν
δούρατ’ ἀνασχόμενοι·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ithys Danaōn brisantes ebēsan
dourat’ anaschomenoi·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they straight at the Danaans, bearing down, went,
spears holding up;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they went, bearing down straight at the Danaans, with their spears held up;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Trojans and allies who heard Hector. ἰθύς with the genitive Δαναῶν means ‘straight at the Danaans’. βρίσαντες is the aorist participle of βρίθω ‘be heavy, press with weight’, and ἔβησαν the aorist of βαίνω ‘went’. ἀνασχόμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἀνέχω, ‘holding up’ their spears for the thrust.

sentences.t:
μάλα δέ σφισιν ἔλπετο θυμὸς
νεκρὸν ὑπ’ Αἴαντος ἐρύειν Τελαμωνιάδαο
νήπιοι·
sentences.tr:
mala de sphisin elpeto thymos
nekron hyp’ Aiantos eryein Telamōniadao
nēpioi·
sentences.l:
and greatly their heart hoped
to drag the corpse from under Ajax, Telamon’s-son,
foolish ones!
sentences.i: and their hearts hoped greatly to drag the corpse out from under Ajax, the son of Telamon, foolish as they were!
sentences.n: ἔλπετο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’, with θυμός ‘heart’ as its subject and σφισιν ‘for them’ in the dative. ὑπ’ Αἴαντος ‘from under Ajax’ puts the body under his protection, and Τελαμωνιάδαο is a patronymic in -αο, ‘son of Telamon’. νήπιοι ‘foolish ones’ is the poet’s own comment on the Trojans’ hope.

sentences.t: ἦ τε πολέσσιν ἐπ’ αὐτῷ θυμὸν ἀπηύρα.
sentences.tr: ē te polessin ep’ autōi thymon apēura.
sentences.l: Truly, from many over him the spirit he had taken away.
sentences.i: for in truth he had taken the lives of many over him.
sentences.n: ἦ τε ‘truly’ is a particle of emphasis, giving the reason the hope is foolish. ἀπηύρα is a past tense of ἀπαυράω ‘take away from’, with the loser in the dative (πολέσσιν, epic dative plural ‘from many’) and the thing taken in the accusative (θυμόν); θυμός is the spirit as the breath of life, so ‘took away the spirit’ means ‘killed’. ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘over him’ is the body of Patroclus, and Ajax is the subject: he had already killed many Trojans fighting over it.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ Αἴας εἶπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸν Μενέλαον·
sentences.tr: kai tot’ ar’ Aias eipe boēn agathon Menelaon·
sentences.l: And then Ajax said to Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Then Ajax said to Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.n: A line that introduces a new speaker. εἶπε with the accusative of the person (βοὴν ἀγαθὸν Μενέλαον) is ‘said to’. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is the stock epithet of Menelaus, with βοήν as an accusative of respect. This is Telamon’s son Ajax, named at 235.

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπον ὦ Μενέλαε διοτρεφὲς οὐκέτι νῶϊ
ἔλπομαι αὐτώ περ νοστησέμεν ἐκ πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
ō pepon ō Menelae diotrephes ouketi nōï
elpomai autō per nostēsemen ek polemoio.
sentences.l:
“O good one, O Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, no longer us two
do I expect, even ourselves, to return from the war;
sentences.i: “My good fellow, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured one, I no longer expect even we two ourselves to get back home from the war;
sentences.n: ὦ πέπον ‘my good fellow’ is the table’s address; the meaning of πέπον is not known. διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured one’ is the table’s epithet, here a vocative. νῶϊ and αὐτώ are duals, ‘we two’ and ‘we two ourselves’, with περ ‘even’: not even the two of us. ἔλπομαι here is ‘expect’, of a bad prospect, with the future infinitive νοστησέμεν (Attic νοστήσειν) ‘to get home’.
sentences.mark: Ajax sends Menelaus to call the leaders

sentences.t:
οὔ τι τόσον νέκυος περιδείδια Πατρόκλοιο,
ὅς κε τάχα Τρώων κορέει κύνας ἠδ’ οἰωνούς,
sentences.tr:
ou ti toson nekyos perideidia Patrokloio,
hos ke tacha Trōōn koreei kynas ēd’ oiōnous,
sentences.l:
not at all so much for the corpse of Patroclus do I fear,
who soon will sate the dogs of the Trojans and the birds,
sentences.i: I am not so afraid for the body of Patroclus, who will soon glut the dogs of the Trojans and the birds,
sentences.n: περιδείδια is a perfect with present sense, ‘I fear greatly for’, taking the genitive of what one fears for (νέκυος … Πατρόκλοιο, with the epic genitive -οιο). οὔ τι τόσον ‘not so much’ opens a comparison finished by ὅσσον ‘as much as’ in 242. ὅς refers to Patroclus, and κορέει is a future of κορέννυμι ‘sate’ with its σ dropped; with κε it marks what is bound to come: he ‘will sate’ them. Τρώων goes with κύνας ‘dogs’, and ἠδ’ οἰωνούς adds the birds.

sentences.t:
ὅσσον ἐμῇ κεφαλῇ περιδείδια μή τι πάθῃσι,
καὶ σῇ,
sentences.tr:
hosson emēi kephalēi perideidia mē ti pathēisi,
kai sēi,
sentences.l:
as much as for my head I fear, lest it suffer something,
and for yours,
sentences.i: as I fear for my head, lest some harm come to it, and for yours,
sentences.n: ὅσσον completes the comparison: not so much for the corpse as for the two of them. κεφαλῇ ‘head’ stands for the person, as often, so ‘for my own self’, and σῇ in the next words is ‘your’ head. μή with the subjunctive πάθῃσι (epic -σι) after a verb of fearing means ‘lest it suffer’, and τι ‘anything’ makes it ‘some harm’.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ πολέμοιο νέφος περὶ πάντα καλύπτει
Ἕκτωρ,
sentences.tr:
epei polemoio nephos peri panta kalyptei
Hektōr,
sentences.l:
since the cloud of war around everything covers,
Hector,
sentences.i: since the cloud of war, Hector, covers everything round about,
sentences.n: νέφος πολέμοιο ‘cloud of war’ is the dark mass of battle, as with the Trojans’ ‘dark cloud’ at 16.66. καλύπτει ‘covers’ takes περὶ πάντα ‘round about everything’. Ἕκτωρ is held back to the end and stands in apposition to νέφος: Hector is the cloud. ἐπεί means ‘since’.

sentences.t: ἡμῖν δ’ αὖτ’ ἀναφαίνεται αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος.
sentences.tr: hēmin d’ aut’ anaphainetai aipys olethros.
sentences.l: and to us in turn appears steep destruction.
sentences.i: and for us in turn steep destruction appears.
sentences.n: ἡμῖν δ’ αὖτ’ ‘and for us in turn’ sets our case against Hector’s cloud. ἀναφαίνεται ‘shows itself, appears’, and αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος ‘steep destruction’ is the table’s phrase: destruction like a sheer cliff.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἀριστῆας Δαναῶν κάλει, ἤν τις ἀκούσῃ.
sentences.tr: all’ ag’ aristēas Danaōn kalei, ēn tis akousēi.
sentences.l: But come, call the best men of the Danaans, if anyone will hear.”
sentences.i: But come, call the best men of the Danaans, in case any of them hears.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ‘but come’ (ἄγε, an imperative) calls for action. ἀριστῆας are ‘the best men’, the champions, and κάλει is the present imperative of καλέω ‘call’. ἤν = ἐάν, with the aorist subjunctive ἀκούσῃ, ‘if anyone should hear’. Ajax’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος,
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse boēn agathos Menelaos,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Menelaus, good at the war-cry, did not disobey;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Ajax’ speech. οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘and did not disobey’ (aorist of ἀπιθέω) is the stock phrase for prompt obedience, as at 2.166, and the subject Menelaus waits until the end of the line.

sentences.t: ἤϋσεν δὲ διαπρύσιον Δαναοῖσι γεγωνώς·
sentences.tr: ēÿsen de diaprysion Danaoisi gegōnōs·
sentences.l: And he shouted, piercingly, calling to the Danaans:
sentences.i: and he shouted piercingly, calling out to the Danaans:
sentences.n: ἤϋσεν is the aorist of ἠϋω ‘shout’. γεγωνώς is the perfect participle of γεγωνέω ‘call out’, and διαπρύσιον ‘piercingly’ is an adverb. Δαναοῖσι is the epic dative plural, ‘to the Danaans’.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
οἵ τε παρ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃς Ἀγαμέμνονι καὶ Μενελάῳ
δήμια πίνουσιν καὶ σημαίνουσιν ἕκαστος
λαοῖς·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi Argeiōn hēgētores ēde medontes
hoi te par’ Atreïdēis Agamemnoni kai Menelaōi
dēmia pinousin kai sēmainousin hekastos
laois·
sentences.l:
“O friends, leaders and lords of the Argives,
who beside the Atreus’-sons, Agamemnon and Menelaus,
the people’s wine drink, and give orders, each one,
to the peoples;
sentences.i: “Friends, leaders and lords of the Argives, you who drink the people’s wine beside the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus, and each give orders to his people;
sentences.n: The address is the same as Nestor’s at 2.79. οἵ τε is the general relative ‘who’, and παρ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃς ‘beside the sons of Atreus’ is a dative plural in -ῃς, ‘in their company’. δήμια is ‘the people’s’, neuter plural, with the noun ‘wine’ understood: the wine that the community provides to its leaders as an honour. σημαίνουσιν ‘give orders’, with ἕκαστος ‘each one’ in apposition to the relative.

sentences.t: ἐκ δὲ Διὸς τιμὴ καὶ κῦδος ὀπηδεῖ.
sentences.tr: ek de Dios timē kai kydos opēdei.
sentences.l: and from Zeus honour and glory attend.
sentences.i: and honour and glory from Zeus attend them.
sentences.n: ἐκ Διός ‘from Zeus’: a leader’s honour comes from Zeus. ὀπηδεῖ is ‘attends, goes with’ and is singular, agreeing with the nearer of its two subjects. τιμή is ‘honour’ and κῦδος ‘glory’.

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον δέ μοί ἐστι διασκοπιᾶσθαι ἕκαστον
ἡγεμόνων·
sentences.tr:
argaleon de moi esti diaskopiasthai hekaston
hēgemonōn·
sentences.l:
And hard for me it is to look over each
of the leaders;
sentences.i: But it is hard for me to look over each one of the leaders;
sentences.n: ἀργαλέον ‘hard, troublesome’ takes the infinitive διασκοπιᾶσθαι ‘to look through, scan’; ἕκαστον ἡγεμόνων is ‘each of the leaders’, a partitive genitive. Menelaus explains why he cannot go searching for the leaders himself.

sentences.t: τόσση γὰρ ἔρις πολέμοιο δέδηεν·
sentences.tr: tossē gar eris polemoio dedēen·
sentences.l: for so great a strife of war is ablaze;
sentences.i: for so great a strife of war is blazing;
sentences.n: τόσση is τόση ‘so great’ with the doubled σ. δέδηεν is the perfect of δαίω ‘burn’, with present sense ‘is ablaze’, and ἔρις πολέμοιο is ‘strife of war’: the fighting is a fire that spreads everywhere.

sentences.t: ἀλλά τις αὐτὸς ἴτω,
sentences.tr: alla tis autos itō,
sentences.l: but let someone himself go,
sentences.i: but let someone go himself,
sentences.n: ἴτω is the third-person imperative of εἶμι ‘go’. αὐτός ‘himself’ means in person; Menelaus asks a leader to come of his own accord.

sentences.t:
νεμεσιζέσθω δ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
Πάτροκλον Τρῳῇσι κυσὶν μέλπηθρα γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
nemesizesthō d’ eni thymōi
Patroklon Trōiēisi kysin melpēthra genesthai.
sentences.l:
and let him feel resentment in his heart
that Patroclus become playthings for Trojan dogs.”
sentences.i: and let him feel resentment in his heart that Patroclus should become the playthings of Trojan dogs.”
sentences.n: νεμεσιζέσθω is the third-person imperative of νεμεσίζομαι ‘feel resentment’, the table’s ‘resentment’, taking an accusative and infinitive: ‘that Patroclus become’. μέλπηθρα ‘playthings’ is related to μέλπω ‘sing and dance’, and the sense of the noun is inferred; it is plural though Patroclus is one man. Τρῳῇσι is a feminine adjective in the dative plural agreeing with κυσίν ‘dogs’, so ‘Trojan bitches’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ὀξὺ δ’ ἄκουσεν Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, oxy d’ akousen Oïlēos tachys Aias·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and keenly heard swift Ajax, son of Oileus;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and swift Ajax, son of Oileus, heard him keenly;
sentences.n: This is the lesser Ajax, ‘swift Ajax, son of Oileus’ (the table’s phrase), to be told from Telamon’s son Ajax, who spoke earlier. Ὀϊλῆος is a genitive in epic -ηος. ὀξύ ‘keenly’ is a neuter adjective used as an adverb, and ὣς ἔφατ’ is again the closing formula of a speech.

sentences.t: πρῶτος δ’ ἀντίος ἦλθε θέων ἀνὰ δηϊοτῆτα,
sentences.tr: prōtos d’ antios ēlthe theōn ana dēïotēta,
sentences.l: and first, face to face, he came, running through the fighting,
sentences.i: and he was the first to come to meet him, running through the fighting,
sentences.n: πρῶτος ‘first’ of the leaders to answer the call. ἀντίος ‘face to face’ says that he runs to meet Menelaus, and θέων is the present participle of θέω ‘run’. ἀνὰ δηϊοτῆτα is ‘up through the fighting’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ μετ’ Ἰδομενεὺς καὶ ὀπάων Ἰδομενῆος
Μηριόνης ἀτάλαντος Ἐνυαλίῳ ἀνδρειφόντῃ.
sentences.tr:
ton de met’ Idomeneus kai opaōn Idomenēos
Mērionēs atalantos Enyaliōi andreiphontēi.
sentences.l:
and after him Idomeneus and Idomeneus’ follower,
Meriones, the equal of Enyalius, killer of men.
sentences.i: and after him Idomeneus and Idomeneus’ follower Meriones, the equal of Enyalius, killer of men.
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is Ajax son of Oileus, and μετά with the accusative means ‘after’. The ὀπάων ‘follower’ is Meriones, whose name is held back to 259. ἀτάλαντος ‘equal’ takes the dative Ἐνυαλίῳ, the war-god, and ἀνδρειφόντῃ ‘killer of men’ is the god’s epithet. Line 259 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee, and Ἐνυαλίῳ has to be scanned with synizesis, the -ιῳ as one syllable.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων τίς κεν ᾗσι φρεσὶν οὐνόματ’ εἴποι,
ὅσσοι δὴ μετόπισθε μάχην ἤγειραν Ἀχαιῶν;
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ allōn tis ken hēisi phresin ounomat’ eipoi,
hossoi dē metopisthe machēn ēgeiran Achaiōn;
sentences.l:
And of the others, who in his own wits could tell the names,
all those who behind them roused the battle of the Achaeans?
sentences.i: And of the rest, who could name from his own mind all those who came behind them and roused the fighting of the Achaeans?
sentences.n: The poet asks the question himself: ‘who could say their names’ (κεν with the optative εἴποι, a possibility) from his own wits, without the Muse’s help; compare his appeal to the Muses at 2.484–492. οὐνόματ’ is οὐνόματα, Ionic for ὀνόματα. μετόπισθε ‘behind, afterwards’ is here ‘behind them’. ἤγειραν is the aorist of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’ (spelled like the ἤγειρα of 222), with μάχην ‘battle’.

sentences.t: Τρῶες δὲ προὔτυψαν ἀολλέες· ἦρχε δ’ ἄρ’ Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.tr: Trōes de proutypsan aollees· ērche d’ ar’ Hektōr.
sentences.l: And the Trojans pressed forward in a close mass; and led, then, Hector.
sentences.i: And the Trojans pressed forward in a close mass, with Hector leading them.
sentences.n: προὔτυψαν (= προέτυψαν) is the aorist of a verb meaning ‘press forward, strike forward’. ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ describes the Trojans massed together. ἦρχε ‘led’ is the imperfect of ἄρχω, and ἄρ’ is a light ‘then’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἐπὶ προχοῇσι διιπετέος ποταμοῖο
βέβρυχεν μέγα κῦμα ποτὶ ῥόον,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ epi prochoēisi diipeteos potamoio
bebrychen mega kyma poti rhoon,
sentences.l:
And as when at the outflows of a Zeus-fallen river
roars a great wave against the stream,
sentences.i: As when, at the mouths of a river fallen from Zeus, a great wave roars against the current,
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ‘and as when’ opens a simile that runs to 266, where τόσσῃ ‘so’ answers it. προχοῇσι is an epic dative plural, ‘outpourings, river-mouths’. διιπετέος ‘fallen from Zeus’ is the epithet of rivers, and the old gloss ‘rain-fed’ shows that its meaning is not certain. βέβρυχεν is a perfect with present sense, ‘roars’, and ποτὶ ῥόον is ‘against the stream’.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ τ’ ἄκραι
ἠϊόνες βοόωσιν ἐρευγομένης ἁλὸς ἔξω,
sentences.tr:
amphi de t’ akrai
ēïones booōsin ereugomenēs halos exō,
sentences.l:
and round about the jutting
beaches bellow, as the sea belches outward,
sentences.i: and round about, the jutting beaches bellow as the sea belches outward,
sentences.n: ἠϊόνες ‘beaches’ and ἄκραι ‘jutting’ together make headlands that stand out into the water. βοόωσιν is the uncontracted present of βοάω ‘shout, roar’. ἐρευγομένης ἁλὸς ἔξω is a genitive absolute, ‘the sea belching out’: the surf is thrown up on the land as the river and sea meet.

sentences.t: τόσσῃ ἄρα Τρῶες ἰαχῇ ἴσαν.
sentences.tr: tossēi ara Trōes iachēi isan.
sentences.l: with so great a cry, then, the Trojans went.
sentences.i: with so great a cry the Trojans came on.
sentences.n: τόσσῃ answers the simile’s ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ of 263, ‘as … so’. ἰαχῇ is the dative of ἰαχή ‘cry’, and ἴσαν the imperfect of εἶμι, ‘they went’, so ‘they advanced’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἕστασαν ἀμφὶ Μενοιτιάδῃ ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντες
φραχθέντες σάκεσιν χαλκήρεσιν·
sentences.tr:
autar Achaioi
hestasan amphi Menoitiadēi hena thymon echontes
phrachthentes sakesin chalkēresin·
sentences.i: but the Achaeans stood round the son of Menoetius with one heart, fenced in with their bronze-fitted shields;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ sets the Achaeans against the Trojans’ roar. ἕστασαν is the old pluperfect ‘were standing’ (Attic εἱστήκεσαν), and Μενοιτιάδῃ the dative of Μενοιτιάδης ‘son of Menoetius’, Patroclus. ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντες ‘with one heart’ means of one mind. φραχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of φράσσω ‘fence in’, and χαλκήρεσιν ‘bronze-fitted’ is the table’s word.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρά σφι
λαμπρῇσιν κορύθεσσι Κρονίων ἠέρα πολλὴν
χεῦ’,
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ara sphi
lamprēisin korythessi Kroniōn ēera pollēn
cheu’,
sentences.l:
and around them
on their bright helmets the son of Cronus much mist
poured,
sentences.i: and the son of Cronus poured a thick mist round them, over their bright helmets,
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … σφι is ‘around them’ (σφι the epic dative), and λαμπρῇσιν κορύθεσσι ‘bright helmets’ is a dative of place, ‘on their helmets’. ἠέρα πολλήν is ‘much mist’, a thick mist. χεῦ’ is the unaugmented aorist of χέω ‘pour’ with its last vowel dropped. The mist is Zeus’s, and the next lines say why he does this.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ Μενοιτιάδην ἔχθαιρε πάρος γε,
ὄφρα ζωὸς ἐὼν θεράπων ἦν Αἰακίδαο·
sentences.tr:
epei oude Menoitiadēn echthaire paros ge,
ophra zōos eōn therapōn ēn Aiakidao·
sentences.l:
since not even Menoetius’-son did he hate before,
while, being alive, he was the attendant of the descendant of Aeacus;
sentences.i: for he had not hated the son of Menoetius before either, while still alive he was the attendant of the descendant of Aeacus;
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ οὐδέ … πάρος γε ‘since not even … before’: Zeus had not hated Patroclus earlier, as long as he lived. ἔχθαιρε is the imperfect of ἐχθαίρω ‘hate’. ὄφρα ζωὸς ἐών is ‘while, being alive’ (ἐών is Homeric for ὤν), and θεράπων ‘attendant’ is the table’s word; Αἰακίδαο is Achilles, ‘descendant of Aeacus’ (his grandfather).

sentences.t:
μίσησεν δ’ ἄρα μιν δηΐων κυσὶ κύρμα γενέσθαι
Τρῳῇσιν·
sentences.tr:
misēsen d’ ara min dēïōn kysi kyrma genesthai
Trōiēisin·
sentences.l:
and he loathed that he become spoil for the dogs of the enemy,
Trojan ones;
sentences.i: and he loathed that he should become spoil for the dogs of his enemies, Trojan dogs;
sentences.n: μίσησεν is the aorist of μισέω ‘loathe’; μιν ‘him’ is Patroclus, who is also the subject of the infinitive γενέσθαι ‘to become’. κύρμα is ‘spoil’, a thing found or caught, as in the table’s ‘prey and spoil’. δηΐων ‘of the enemy’ is the epic genitive plural of δήϊος, and Τρῳῇσιν is a feminine adjective agreeing with κυσί ‘dogs’, as at 255.

sentences.t: τὼ καί οἱ ἀμυνέμεν ὦρσεν ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr: tō kai hoi amynemen ōrsen hetairous.
sentences.l: therefore also for him to ward off he roused companions.
sentences.i: and so he also roused companions to defend him.
sentences.n: τώ ‘therefore’ again, as at 227, and καί ‘also’. οἱ ‘for him’ is a dative of advantage, and ἀμυνέμεν (= ἀμύνειν) ‘to ward off, defend’ has no stated object: the harm is understood. ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’.

sentences.t: ὦσαν δὲ πρότεροι Τρῶες ἑλίκωπας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr: ōsan de proteroi Trōes helikōpas Achaious·
sentences.l: And pushed first the Trojans the quick-eyed Achaeans;
sentences.i: The Trojans were the first to push the quick-eyed Achaeans back;
sentences.n: πρότεροι ‘first, earlier’ agrees with Τρῶες: they were the first to push. ὦσαν is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’. ἑλίκωπας ‘quick-eyed’ is the masculine of the epithet ἑλικῶπις, and its sense is disputed. The Achaeans are driven back from the body.

sentences.t: νεκρὸν δὲ προλιπόντες ὑπέτρεσαν,
sentences.tr: nekron de prolipontes hypetresan,
sentences.l: and the corpse leaving, they took fright,
sentences.i: and, leaving the corpse, they took fright,
sentences.n: προλιπόντες is the aorist participle ‘leaving behind’, and ὑπέτρεσαν ‘took fright’ the table’s τρέω with ὑπο- ‘back from’. The subject, the Achaeans, is not named after the Trojans of the line above.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τιν’ αὐτῶν
Τρῶες ὑπέρθυμοι ἕλον ἔγχεσιν ἱέμενοί περ,
sentences.tr:
oude tin’ autōn
Trōes hyperthymoi helon enchesin hiemenoi per,
sentences.l:
and not one of them
the high-spirited Trojans took with spears, though eager,
sentences.i: and none of them did the high-spirited Trojans kill with their spears, eager though they were,
sentences.n: οὐδέ τιν’ αὐτῶν ‘and not one of them’ is the object. ἕλον is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, which with a man as object means ‘kill’. ὑπέρθυμοι ‘high-spirited’ is the table’s epithet, and ἱέμενοί περ is a present middle participle of ἵημι, ‘eager’, with περ ‘though’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ νέκυν ἐρύοντο·
sentences.tr: alla nekyn eryonto·
sentences.l: but the corpse they were dragging;
sentences.i: but they went on dragging the corpse;
sentences.n: The subject is again the Trojans. ἐρύοντο is the imperfect middle of ἐρύω ‘drag’, the middle voice meaning ‘drag to themselves’. The unit is short because the next clause turns back to the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
μίνυνθα δὲ καὶ τοῦ Ἀχαιοὶ
μέλλον ἀπέσσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
minyntha de kai tou Achaioi
mellon apessesthai·
sentences.l:
and briefly even from it the Achaeans
were to be away;
sentences.i: but for only a little while were the Achaeans to be parted from it;
sentences.n: μίνυνθα ‘for a little while’ is the key word: the Achaeans were to be away from the corpse only briefly, and the next words say why. τοῦ ‘from it’ is a genitive of separation (the corpse), μέλλον is ἔμελλον ‘were going to’, and ἀπέσσεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἄπειμι, ‘be away’.

sentences.t:
μάλα γάρ σφεας ὦκ’ ἐλέλιξεν
Αἴας,
sentences.tr:
mala gar spheas ōk’ elelixen
Aias,
sentences.l:
for very quickly them he whirled round,
Ajax,
sentences.i: for very quickly Ajax wheeled them round,
sentences.n: μάλα γάρ gives the reason, ‘for very’, and ὦκ’ is ὦκα ‘quickly’. σφεας is the epic accusative plural ‘them’, the Achaeans. ἐλέλιξεν is the aorist of ἐλελίζω, here ‘whirl round, make wheel about’: Ajax swings the retreating men to face the enemy again. The table’s ‘shook’ at 1.530 is the same verb in its other sense, ‘make tremble’. This is the greater Ajax, named in full at 284.

sentences.t:
ὃς περὶ μὲν εἶδος, περὶ δ’ ἔργα τέτυκτο
τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν μετ’ ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.tr:
hos peri men eidos, peri d’ erga tetykto
tōn allōn Danaōn met’ amymona Pēleïōna.
sentences.l:
who in form beyond, and in deeds beyond, was fashioned
above the other Danaans, after the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.i: who surpassed the other Danaans in form and in deeds, after the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.n: περὶ … περὶ are adverbs, ‘beyond’, and τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘was fashioned’: a man made beyond the rest in looks and deeds, with τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν as the genitive of comparison. μετ’ ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα ‘after the blameless son of Peleus’ makes Achilles the one better man. The closing words are the same as those said of Nireus at 2.674.

sentences.t:
ἴθυσεν δὲ διὰ προμάχων συῒ εἴκελος ἀλκὴν
καπρίῳ,
sentences.tr:
ithysen de dia promachōn syï eikelos alkēn
kapriōi,
sentences.l:
And he rushed through the front-fighters, like a swine in might,
a boar,
sentences.i: And he rushed through the foremost fighters, like a wild boar in might,
sentences.n: ἴθυσεν is the aorist of ἰθύω ‘rush straight’, and διὰ προμάχων ‘through the front-fighters’ is the men in the first line. συῒ εἴκελος ἀλκήν is ‘like a boar in might’, with ἀλκήν an accusative of respect, as at 4.253; καπρίῳ ‘a boar’ is a second noun set beside σύς, as at 11.293, and together they give ‘wild boar’.

sentences.t:
ὅς τ’ ἐν ὄρεσσι κύνας θαλερούς τ’ αἰζηοὺς
ῥηϊδίως ἐκέδασσεν, ἑλιξάμενος διὰ βήσσας·
sentences.tr:
hos t’ en oressi kynas thalerous t’ aizēous
rhēïdiōs ekedassen, helixamenos dia bēssas·
sentences.l:
who in the mountains dogs and flourishing vigorous young men
easily scattered, having wheeled round through the glens;
sentences.i: who in the mountains easily scatters dogs and flourishing young men, wheeling round through the glens;
sentences.n: ὅς τ’ … ἐκέδασσεν is a general statement told in the aorist (the gnomic aorist): what a boar does, so the free English has the present ‘scatters’. κύνας ‘dogs’ and αἰζηούς ‘vigorous young men’ are the two objects, with θαλερούς ‘flourishing’ (the table’s word) describing the men. ἑλιξάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἑλίσσω ‘turn, wheel’, the boar swinging round on its pursuers; βήσσας are ‘glens, wooded valleys’.

sentences.t:
ὣς υἱὸς Τελαμῶνος ἀγαυοῦ φαίδιμος Αἴας
ῥεῖα μετεισάμενος Τρώων ἐκέδασσε φάλαγγας
οἳ περὶ Πατρόκλῳ βέβασαν, φρόνεον δὲ μάλιστα
ἄστυ πότι σφέτερον ἐρύειν καὶ κῦδος ἀρέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs huios Telamōnos agauou phaidimos Aias
rheia meteisamenos Trōōn ekedasse phalangas
hoi peri Patroklōi bebasan, phroneon de malista
asty poti spheteron eryein kai kydos aresthai.
sentences.l:
so the son of Telamon the noble, glorious Ajax,
easily, rushing in among them, scattered the battle-lines of the Trojans,
who had taken their stand about Patroclus, and were thinking most of all
to drag him to their own city and to win glory.
sentences.i: So glorious Ajax, the son of noble Telamon, rushing in among them, easily scattered the battle-lines of the Trojans who stood about Patroclus and were most intent on dragging him to their own city and winning glory.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ answers the boar simile of 281–283: Ajax is the boar, the Trojans the dogs and men. υἱὸς Τελαμῶνος ἀγαυοῦ is ‘son of noble Telamon’, with φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ (the table’s word) and the greater Ajax. μετεισάμενος is an aorist middle participle of the verb behind ἐείσατο ‘rushed’, with μετά ‘among’. βέβασαν is an unaugmented pluperfect, ‘had taken their stand’ (Attic ἐβεβήκεσαν), and φρόνεον ‘were thinking’ takes the infinitives ἐρύειν ‘to drag’ (the corpse understood) and ἀρέσθαι ‘to win’ (aorist middle of αἴρομαι). πότι is πρός, ‘to’.
